title: Does a Cracked Tooth Always Need a Root Canal?
metaTitle: Does a Cracked Tooth Always Need a Root Canal?

bodyHtml:
Does a cracked tooth always need a root canal?

No. A cracked tooth does not automatically require a root canal. What treatment you need depends mainly on how deep the crack goes and whether it has reached the pulp, the living tissue inside the tooth. Shallow cracks may need only monitoring, smoothing, or a bonded filling. Deeper cracks that affect the biting surface often need a crown to hold the tooth together, while cracks that extend into the pulp or down the root may call for root canal treatment or, in some cases, extraction. Only an examination, usually with X-rays and bite testing, can tell which situation you are in.

Teeth crack for all sorts of reasons: biting something hard, grinding or clenching, large old fillings, or simply years of wear. Because the word "crack" covers everything from a harmless surface line to a split that threatens the whole tooth, it helps to understand the range.

The spectrum of cracks and what they usually mean

Craze lines are tiny cracks in the outer enamel. They are common in adults, usually painless, and typically need no treatment beyond keeping an eye on them.

A cracked tooth that extends toward the gum but has not split apart often causes pain when you bite and release, or sensitivity to temperature. If the crack has not reached the pulp, a crown may protect it. If the pulp is involved, root canal treatment may be recommended before the crown.

A fractured cusp, where a piece of the chewing surface breaks off, frequently happens around a large filling. Many of these are restored with a new filling or crown and do not need a root canal unless the pulp is affected.

A split tooth or vertical root fracture is more serious. When a crack travels down into the root and separates segments of the tooth, saving it may not be possible, and extraction can be the realistic option. Early assessment improves the chance of keeping more of the tooth.

How a dentist decides

Diagnosing cracks can be tricky because they do not always show clearly on X-rays. A dentist may use a bite stick to reproduce the pain, special dyes, magnification, or a careful look under the gumline. They will ask when the tooth hurts: sharp pain on biting that disappears quickly points toward a crack, while lingering throbbing pain can suggest the pulp is inflamed or infected. The goal is to match the treatment to the depth and behaviour of the crack rather than jumping straight to the most involved option.

Why act sooner rather than later?

Cracks tend to grow. A line that only needs a crown today could extend into the root if you keep chewing on it for months. Treating a crack earlier often means a simpler, more tooth-preserving solution, whereas waiting can narrow the options. If a tooth is newly sensitive to biting or temperature, it is worth having it looked at before symptoms escalate.

Will I feel the tooth is "dead" after a root canal for a crack?

If a crack has inflamed or infected the pulp, root canal treatment removes that tissue and the tooth no longer senses hot and cold. The tooth itself stays in place and continues to function, usually protected by a crown. Measured expectations matter here: outcomes depend on how far the crack extends, and your dentist will assess whether the tooth can be reliably restored.

Protecting a cracked tooth in Markham

If you suspect a cracked tooth, a timely exam is the best way to understand your choices and avoid a bigger problem later. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, offers restorative and root canal care at her Markham practice and can help you weigh options from a simple filling to a crown or root canal. You can read more about the practice at Smile Dental Arts Centre, and their overview of restorative treatment options explains how damaged teeth are commonly rebuilt. For patients across the GTA, including those in North York considering care in Markham, the key message is reassuring: many cracked teeth are saved without a root canal, and the right treatment depends on what the examination finds.
